To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
guanidinoacetic acid inhibits the activities of NTPDase 1, 5'-NT, and AChE in vitro in rat brain synaptosomes, blood, and platelets.

guanidinoacetic acid (GAA) inhibits NTPDase activity in the synaptosome fraction from cerebral cortex and platelet, and stimulates 5'-nucelotidase activity in both fractions, but inhibits acetylcholinestrase activity only in blood.

the NTPDases, 5'-Nucleotidases and Acetylcholinesterases activities were inhibited by guanidinoacetic acid in the cerebral cortex and blood of rats, while in the platelets the activities of these three enzymes were stimulated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of guanidinobutyric acid in the metabolism of purine nucleoside triphosphate and the activity of acetylcholinestrase in tissues from the adult rats.
the effects of GAA on NTPDase/5'-nucleotide and acetylcholine esterase activities in synaptosomes, blood and platelets.

the effects of guanidinopropionic acid and guanidinoacetic acid on the activities of enzymes involved in the hydrolysis of adenine nucleotides in the synaptosomal membrane, platelets and erythrocytes of the rat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the in vitro effect in the activities of NTPDase/5'-nucleotide and acetylcholine esterase in tissues from adult rat are dependent on GAA concentration.
the in vitro effects of GAA on NTPDase/5'-nucleotide/ acetylcholinestase activity are not consistent in the three studied tissues.

GAA, at concentrations of 100 microM or less, does not seem to be able to alter the activities of NTPDase/5'-nucleotide or acetylcholinestease in the synaptosomal fraction, while in the platelet fraction, GAA may be able to alter these enzymes at lower concentrations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GAA inhibits NTPDase1 activity in platelets but stimulates it in synaptosomes.

the in vitro effect caused by guanidinoacetic acid (GAA) in NTPDases, 5'-Nucleotidase, Acetylcholinesteras activities in tissues from adult rat is different from the effects observed in GAMT deficient patients, which is probably caused by differences in the concentrations of GAA between patients and the in vitro experiments.
GAA has different effects on the NTPDases, 5'-Nucleotidase, and acetylchlinesterase activities in blood and brain tissues.
The main takeaway from our work is that
guanidinoacetic acid (GAA) can alter the activity of enzymes involved in purinergic neurotransmission, and that these effects can be tissue specific.
